rv.q: This is the Broadway show of the fall that some will claim to dislike and yet most everyone will enjoy, even if that has to be in secret.
The song is such a ridiculous rush that it pretty much justifies the whole project.

The new production from director Michael Mayer has the air of peculiar novelty amped to arena-style proportions: Come for the Broadway MVPs wailing to high heaven, shrug as the story ceases to make much sense.
In the unending battle between sincerity and snark, I’m afraid I have to call this particular showdown a draw.
Parts of the show are absolutely thrilling and parts are flat at best, aggressively dumb at worst.

Alas, the debate of whether ‘Chess’ can be saved or fixed must continue, for this is likely not the best iteration of the material. What Florence sings rings true for ‘Chess’ overall: ‘I’ve still a lot to prove; there must be more I could achieve.
The musical wilts under the weight of its many bombastic numbers and passages of clichéd dialogue.
Once again, the show blows its assets; shackled to storytelling that is arguably worse than ever, Chess goes down in forfeit.

With hardly any helpful staging from director Michael Mayer, who has developed an EpiPen-level allergy to good shows, the endless production becomes totally reliant on the amped-up singing of leads Lea Michele, Aaron Tveit and Nicholas Christopher to give it a boost.

If you’ve never seen, or heard, Chess, trust us. Every song is a banger, and the stars—Nicholas Christopher as Russian chess champion Anatoly Sergievsky, Aaron Tveit as American champ Freddie Trumper, and Lea Michele as Florence Vassy, a top chess strategist and the woman loved by both—know it.
For all its lingering structural flaws, this Chess ultimately triumphs on the strength of its performances, its visual sophistication, and its renewed dramatic urgency.
Their collective vocal power is so striking, it may very well be the best heard on Broadway right now.

Giving what I think is his best-ever Broadway performance – actually making us feel sorry for the difficult Freddie – Tveit stops Act II in its tracks with his extraordinary rendition of the ultra-difficult ‘Pity the Child’… Frankly, for all its great songs, ‘Chess’ contains a few too many clunkers… Still, thanks to its superb stars, ‘Chess’ rem...
Some of their updates don't work... but some do
Equal parts demented and exhilarating, this infamously troubled 'Cold War Musical' is almost certainly unfixable.
But once again, it doesn't come together.
As drama, “Chess” remains a puzzle.
Whether or not Chess works as a musical, this rare revival delivers exactly what you paid for: Tveit, Michele, Christopher, and Cruz belt their faces off and look sexy as hell while doing it.

In the end, this Chess may belt to the rafters and flatter the senses, but its stumbling book and cut-out characters keep it from delivering a real checkmate—leaving you admiring the music more than caring who captures the king.

It’s a smugly satisfied approach that would be borderline intolerable if it weren’t for the dazzling constellation of stars that is Lea Michele, Aaron Tveit and Nicholas Christopher, whose full-throated commitment to this tuneful slog may convert even the staunchest of “Chess” agnostics.

Not knowing English might help even more, since too many of the lines and lyrics detract from what’s enjoyable about the show, which is the catchy rock score and the performances by the exciting Broadway pros Aaron Tveit, Lea Michele and Nicholas Christopher.
It is, like many spectacles, good, bad, needily insistent, and unapologetically exhausting.

As for Strong’s new book, it’s even more confusing than Nelson’s rewrite, which never quite made sense of the story’s love triangle – or the show’s chess metaphor regarding the U.S. and the U.S.S.R. blowing each other up.
As for Strong's new book, it's even more confusing than Nelson's rewrite, which never quite made sense of the story's love triangle.
Meanwhile, the promise of an effective staged Chess – if indeed it’s a promise and not a chimera – remains stubbornly out of reach.
In this Chess, the checkmate comes by vocal firepower, and not just once.
That, combined with this unbelievable cast may make this rendering of “Chess” the best to date.
There's some magic happening on Broadway.
Nevertheless, entertainment is the chief value of this sensational Broadway revival.
This production sucked the meaning out of it in an attempt to make it more fun.
And while this revival may not entirely work as a book musical, it succeeds grandly as a glorified staged concert showcasing some of ABBA’s most infectious music.

cn.t: Critics find this Cold War musical still struggles with its famously messy book despite a powerhouse cast, but the ABBA score soars when belted by Michele, Tveit, and Christopher in a campy, concert-style staging that leans into its own ridiculousness.

sg.ra: Imperial's auditorium is rectangular and wider than it is deep, so you lose very little distance moving back from the premium C-G band — and once you clear the mezzanine overhang (which hangs over Orchestra row H) the rake picks up enough to see over heads. Multiple Chess (2026) and Water for Elephants (2024) sitters in rows H-P described a dead-center full-stage view at sub-premium prices; one Chess viewer at Orch C H106 called it 'the best broadway seats I've had.' Seatplan, TickPick, and Headout independently pick this same band as the value tier.

TickPick and Seatplan both explicitly recommend Front Mezz row C and back (centered) over rows A-B, because the Imperial's front-mezz railing sits high enough to clip the stage for front-row sitters — a Water for Elephants viewer at Front Mezz R A401 (self-reported 6'3") wrote 'The bar definitely gets in the way… Avoid.' Rows C-F clear that bar while keeping the whole-stage overhead view that's the main reason to choose mezzanine over orchestra at Imperial.

sg.vl: Steep rake saves the cheap seats
sg.ra: Imperial has no elevators/escalators and the rear mezz is a real climb (one Chess sitter called it 'quite the hike'), but the rake is steep enough that several Chess and Smash viewers reported unobstructed full-stage views from rows A-C even with tall people in front ('Rake is good so most likely no heads blocking the stage,' 'Theater has a good rake so you can see over the person in front of you'). TickPick and Headout both specifically recommend rear-mezz center (not sides) as the cheap-seat sweet spot here.

sg.vl: Under the overhang, far from the action
sg.ra: Imperial is wider than it is deep, so the penalty for sitting far back is real — you lose closeness without gaining much sightline, and the same mid-tier price bracket gets you a few rows forward.

vr.q: What I find most thrilling about this production is how everyone across the board is locked in. There's not a semblance of holding back, which is exactly the assignment for a score that's banger after banger.
Go see Chess for this amazing score, for this amazing staging, and these amazing singers. This is why go see the show for that. I mean, it was worth it.

There is definitely a lot to like about this production, and while I don't think it's going to change anyone's mind about chess, it does deliver a really sleek production that I think highlights all of the things that chess does really well.
if you want to go see something with a compelling story, then I cannot recommend chess as my top option
I cannot impress upon you how important it is that this reworked version of chess is not produced elsewhere after this run. It represents such an epic misinterpretation of the show.
